llm.summary: The skill does what it claims, but its compile-and-flash workflow disables TLS checks and can flash firmware from an unauthenticated server, so users should review it carefully before use.

dimensions.detail: The core purpose is coherent: upload a K10 PlatformIO project to a user-specified compile server, download firmware, and optionally flash a K10. The concern is that the downloaded binaries may be used for device flashing without transport verification or artifact signing.
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

dimensions.detail: The skill requires a user-provided server URL and does not hardcode a destination, but the helper scripts and manual commands consistently use curl with certificate verification disabled and the docs normalize browser certificate bypasses for the server.
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: No automatic install hook, startup hook, or hidden execution path was found; the package consists of skill instructions, references, and user-invoked helper scripts.
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: Remote compilation and firmware flashing are expected for this skill, but they are high-impact actions. The artifacts also include under-warned troubleshooting commands that erase device flash, remove caches/volumes, or loosen serial-device permissions.
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: The skill itself does not persist an agent process or request credentials. Server setup documentation describes Docker volumes, systemd deployment, sudo commands, and an unauthenticated LAN server, which are purpose-related but should be contained to trusted environments.
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

llm.guidance: Install only if you control and trust the K10 compile server and network path. Prefer a real or locally trusted certificate, avoid public exposure because the documented server has no authentication, and treat downloaded firmware as trusted only when you can verify the server. Use Web Serial or flashing options deliberately, and avoid destructive troubleshooting commands unless you understand what data or device state they remove.
llm.findings:
[SC2] expected: Uploading the project archive to a user-selected compile server is central to the skill, but doing it with TLS verification disabled is an avoidable security weakness.
[SC2] expected: Downloading firmware and flash components from the compile server is expected, but the scripts do not verify certificates, signatures, checksums, or provenance before saving or flashing those binaries.
[SQP-2] expected: Cache and temporary-directory cleanup guidance is related to troubleshooting, but it is presented without enough warning about deleted toolchains, cached packages, and rebuild cost.
[SQP-2] expected: Self-signed HTTPS guidance is related to LAN Web Serial requirements, but advising certificate-warning bypasses without strong identity-verification warnings materially weakens the workflow.
[SQP-2] expected: The erase_flash troubleshooting step is relevant to embedded flashing recovery, but it should clearly warn that it wipes the device.
[SQP-2] expected: The chmod 666 serial-port workaround is a purpose-related access fix, but it grants access to all local users and processes and is not least-privilege.
[SQP-2] expected: Removing the Docker PlatformIO volume is relevant to cache reset, but the documentation should warn that it deletes persistent toolchain/cache data.
